Beginners electronics enthusiasts pretty soon discover that electronics components are actually not that precise. Resistors can be 10% tolerance, transistors 20% tolerance, so how are electronics engineers be able to create such precision tools with such bad components?

The answer is that they cripple the amplification of the transistor by placing resistors in such a way that the signal gets reduced. When you take a 500x, 20% tolerance transistor and reduce the output signal 100 times, then you end up with a 5x amplification but a tolerance if 0.2%.
How to increase the accuracy of electronics components (reducing the tolerance).
I am not that smart when it comes to electronic components but isn't there some levels of quality of said transistors/resistors?

Yes you can find better components like 1% resistors but they are more expensive than the 5% ones.

But I want to point out in this discussion is that when you look at schematics, and you wonder what is the fuzz of having specific resistors at the output, it is because they decrease tolerance by weakening the output signal. 20% drift becomes 0.2%. Now you can add a second amplifying just like the first one in series that to bring back the amplification of the signal but this time with less noise.

Imagine this I have a 500x transistor that has a tolerance of 20%. So I build the amplifier that it only amplifies 5x, with the side-effect that I reduce the tolerance to 0.2%. That output signal I again amplify with the same type of 5x amplification so I get 5x5 = 25x amplification and 0.2%+0.2%=0.4% tolerance.

A distributed power supply actually makes the system harder to control and balance. Loads and supplies are managed to prevent outages and equipment damage in the electric grid system. I see rooftop solar as a nightmare situation during large scale events where load must be shed to prevent damage. It sounds great and all in theory, but in practice the whole grid system would need to be revamped to deal with the added dangers of thousands upon thousands of small power sources and shifting loads. Just like wind farms, the system can only use them when the conditions are right. Wind farms are often disconnected from the grid if there is no need for the additional supply or if current will flow into the farm during an equipment or line failure. We should be planning a better system but today's grid was designed around constant supplies from central power plants not transients like solar and wind.

It's only bad for balancing if you have distributed generation and consumption without distributed storage. Once battery-backed solar becomes widespread it will actually be a huge positive for the stability of the grid, since the load on the grid will be reduced from its current bulk power distribution load down to just load sharing and probably some off-peak trickle charging.

You're only thinking about the on paper big block diagram version of how the grid works. Battery backed solar is still transient in nature because the storage capacity is small and easily depleted. The residential distribution system, like the low voltage lines and pole transformers, are the weak link in the system. They are not designed with local control and are generally only for loads not supplies. They can't handle local balancing on their own and will become dangerous under certain conditions if the flow changes direction frequently (load to supply and back and forth). Transformers are going to blow and lines are going to sag. Also, what happens if the grid interface equipment in the solar supplies have frequency drift, phase shifts, power factor correction issues or get hit with dirty inductive loads that draw VARS not Watts? I wouldn't trust a bunch of residential grade equipment to perform at industrial levels and keep the system healthy. Plus, what happens when hardware hackers/enthusiasts (hacker as in person who experiments with technology rather than the bogus mainstream "hacker" definition) starts tweaking their equipment to make it better and actually harms the system instead? As I said before, the system would need to redesigned with distributed supplies in mind. It's just an unfortunate fact that we could not conceive of a future that would not involve large centralized power generation. Your better off planning for a one-per-home solar solution with grid backup and not sharing the supply/load around. It's much safer that way.
